title: The error that comes with birth
source_text: Ὁ μὲν οὖν οὐκ ἐσαφήνισε, πῶς μετὰ γενέσεώς ἐστι πλάνη, οὐδὲ παρέστησεν ὅ τι περ ἐβούλετο, ἵνα κατανοήσωμεν συγκρίνοντες τὰ αὐτοῦ τοῖς ἡμετέροις· οἱ δὲ προφῆται, αἰνιττόμενοι ὅ τι περὶ τῶν γενέσεως πραγμάτων σοφὸν, θυσίαν „περὶ ἁμαρτίας“ λέγουσιν ἀναφέρεσθαι καὶ περὶ τῶν ἄρτι γεγενημένων ὡς οὐ καθαρῶν ἀπὸ ἁμαρτίας. φασὶ δὲ καὶ τό· „ἐν ἀνομίαις συνελήφθην, καὶ ἐν ἁμαρτίαις ἐκίσσησέ με ἡ μήτηρ μου.“ ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀποφαίνονται ὅτι „ἀπηλλοτριώθησαν οἱ ἁμαρτωλοὶ ἀπὸ μήτρας,“ παραδόξως λέγοντες καὶ τό· „ἐπλανήθησαν ἀπὸ γαστρὸς, ἐλάλησαν ψευδῆ.“ οὕτω δὲ πᾶσαν τὴν τῶν αἰσθητῶν διαβάλλουσιν οἱ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς σοφοὶ φύσιν, ὥστε πῇ μὲν ματαιότητα εἰρῆσθαι τὰ σώματα ἐν τῷ „τῇ γὰρ ματαιότητι ἡ κτίσις ὑπετάγη οὐχ ἑκοῦσα ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸν ὑποτάξαντα ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι,“ πῇ δὲ ματαιότητα „ματαιοτήτων“ (ὧν) εἶπεν ὁ ἐκκλησιαστής· „ματαιότης ματαιοτήτων, τὰ πάντα ματαιότης.“ τίς δ᾿ οὕτω διαβέβληκε τὴν ἐνταῦθα τῆς ἀνθρώπου ψυχῆς ζωὴν, ὡς ὁ εἰπών· „πλὴν τὰ σύμπαντα ματαιότης. πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ζῶν;“ οὐ γὰρ ἐδίστασε περὶ τῆς διαφορᾶς τοῦ ζῆν τῆς ψυχῆς ἐνταῦθα καὶ ἔξω τῶν ἐνθάδε, οὐδ᾿ ἔλεγε μέν· τίς οἶδεν εἰ τὸ ζῆν μέν ἐστι κατθανεῖν, τὸ κατθανεῖν δὲ ζῆν; θαῤῥεῖ δὲ λέγειν τὰ ἀληθῆ ἐν τῷ „ἐταπεινώθη εἰς χοῦν ἡ ψυχὴ ἡμῶν“ καὶ „εἰς χοῦν θανάτου κατήγαγές με“· καθὸ καὶ τὸ „τίς με ῥύσεται ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ θανάτου τούτου;“ λέλεκται καὶ τὸ „ὃς μετασχηματίσει τὸ σῶμα τῆς ταπεινώσεως ἡμῶν.“ προφήτης δέ ἐστι καὶ ὁ εἰπὼν τό· „ἐταπείνωσας ἡμᾶς ἐν τόπῳ κακώσεως.“ „κακώσεως“ τόπον λέγων τὸν περίγειον τόπον, ἐφ ὃν ἐκβληθεὶς ἀπὸ τοῦ παραδείσου διὰ τὴν κακίαν ἐλήλυθεν ὁ Ἀδὰμ, ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἄνθρωπος. καὶ ὁ λέγων δὲ ὅτι „βλέπομεν ἄρτι δι᾿ ἐσόπτρου καὶ ἐν αἰνίγματι, τότε δὲ πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον.“ ἔτι δὲ καὶ τό· „ἐνδημοῦντες ἐν τῷ σώματι ἐκδημοῦμεν ἀπὸ τοῦ κυρίου,“ διὸ „εὐδοκοῦμεν ἐκδημῆσαι ἐκ τοῦ σώματος καὶ ἐνδημῆσαι πρὸς τὸν κύριον,“ ὅρα πηλίκα περὶ τῆς διαφόρου ζωῆς τῶν ψυχῶν τεθεωρήκει.
pass_a_gloss: He then did not make clear (σαφηνίζω) how error (πλάνη) is with becoming (γένεσις), nor did he present (παρίστημι) whatever he wished, so that we might understand (κατανοέω) comparing (συγκρίνω) his things with ours; but the prophets, hinting (αἰνίσσομαι) at something wise about the matters of becoming, say a sacrifice (θυσία) 'for sin (περὶ ἁμαρτίας)' is offered (ἀναφέρω) also for those just born (ἄρτι γεγενημένοι), as not pure from sin. And they say also: 'in lawlessnesses (ἀνομίαι) I was conceived (συλλαμβάνω), and in sins my mother conceived/craved (κισσάω) me' (LXX Ps 50:7). But also they declare (ἀποφαίνομαι) that 'sinners were estranged (ἀπαλλοτριόω) from the womb (μήτρα)', saying paradoxically (παραδόξως) also: 'they went astray (πλανάομαι) from the belly (γαστήρ), they spoke lies (ψευδῆ)' (LXX Ps 57:4). So the wise among us slander/disparage (διαβάλλω) the whole nature of the sensibles (αἰσθητά), that in one place bodies (σώματα) are called vanity (ματαιότης) in 'for to vanity the creation (κτίσις) was subjected (ὑποτάσσω) not willing (ἑκών) but through the one who subjected, in hope (ἐλπίς)' (Rom 8:20), in another 'vanity of vanities', (of which) the Preacher (ἐκκλησιαστής) said: 'vanity of vanities, all things vanity' (Eccl 1:2). Who has so disparaged the life (ζωή) of the soul of man here as the one saying: 'nevertheless (πλήν) all things vanity, every man living' (LXX Ps 38:6)? For he did not doubt (διστάζω) about the difference (διαφορά) of the soul's living here and outside the things here, nor did he say: who knows if living is dying (κατθανεῖν), and dying living? But he dares (θαρρέω) to say the true things in 'our soul was humbled (ταπεινόω) to dust (χοῦς)' (LXX Ps 43:26) and 'into dust of death you brought me down (κατάγω)' (LXX Ps 21:16); accordingly also 'who will rescue (ῥύομαι) me from the body of this death' (Rom 7:24) has been said, and 'who will transform (μετασχηματίζω) the body of our humiliation (ταπείνωσις)' (Phil 3:21). A prophet also is the one saying: 'you humbled us in a place of ill-treatment (κάκωσις)' (LXX Ps 43:20), calling 'place of ill-treatment' the region about the earth (περίγειος τόπος), to which, cast out (ἐκβάλλω) of paradise (παράδεισος) through wickedness (κακία), Adam has come, which is man (ἄνθρωπος). And the one saying that 'we see now through a mirror (ἔσοπτρον) and in a riddle (αἴνιγμα), but then face to face' (1 Cor 13:12); and further: 'being at home (ἐνδημέω) in the body we are away (ἐκδημέω) from the Lord', therefore 'we are well pleased (εὐδοκέω) to go away from the body and be at home with the Lord' (2 Cor 5:6, 8): see how great things (πηλίκα) he had contemplated (θεωρέω) about the differing (διάφορος) life of souls.
pass_b_english: He, then, did not make clear how error goes with becoming, nor did he set out whatever he meant, so that we might understand it by comparing his views with ours. But the prophets, hinting at some wise teaching about the things of becoming, say that a sacrifice “for sin” is offered even for those just born, as not pure from sin (Leviticus 12:6–8). They also say: “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 51:5). And they declare as well that “sinners were estranged from the womb,” and they also say, in a surprising way, “they went astray from the belly, they spoke lies” (Psalm 58:3).

So thoroughly do the wise men among us disparage the whole nature of things perceived by the senses that in one place bodies are called vanity, in the words “For the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope” (Romans 8:20), and in another they are called the vanity “of vanities,” as the Preacher said: “Vanity of vanities, all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2). And who has so disparaged the life of the human soul here as he who said, “Nevertheless, all things are vanity, every man living” (Psalm 39:5)? For he had no doubt about the difference between the soul’s life here and its life outside the things of this world, nor did he say, “Who knows whether to live is to die, and to die is to live?” (Euripides, quoted in Plato, Gorgias 492e). Rather, he is bold to speak the truth in the words “our soul was brought low to the dust” (Psalm 44:25) and “you brought me down into the dust of death” (Psalm 22:15).

In keeping with this it has been said, “Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24), and also, “who will transform the body of our lowliness” (Philippians 3:21). He too is a prophet who said, “You brought us low in a place of affliction” (Psalm 44:19), calling the region about the earth a “place of affliction,” the place to which Adam, that is, man, came when he was cast out of paradise because of wickedness (Genesis 3:23–24). And as for him who says, “Now we see through a mirror and in a riddle, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12), and further, “While we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:6), and therefore “we are well pleased to be away from the body and at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8), see how great were the things he had contemplated about the different life of souls.

choices.choice: LXX renumbering: Psalm 51:5 = LXX 50:7; Psalm 58:3 = LXX 57:4; Psalm 39:5 = LXX 38:6 (Hebrew 39:6); Psalm 44:25 = LXX 43:26; Psalm 22:15 = LXX 21:16; Psalm 44:19 = LXX 43:20 (the Hebrew has ‘a place of jackals’; the LXX ‘τόπῳ κακώσεως’ is followed here). ‘ἐκίσσησε’ (κισσάω, to crave as a pregnant woman does) rendered ‘conceived’, the usual sense in this verse. The sin-offering (περὶ ἁμαρτίας) in Leviticus 12:6-8 is offered at the mother’s purification after childbirth; Origen reads it as offered for the newborn, and the English follows his reading. ‘They went astray’ (ἐπλανήθησαν) keeps the link with Celsus’s ‘error’ (πλάνη) in 7.45. ’(ὧν)’ is an editorial supplement and does not affect the sense. The line ‘Who knows whether to live is to die...’ is a fragment of Euripides quoted by Plato at Gorgias 492e; Origen does not name the poet, so ‘Euripides, quoted in Plato’ is the editor’s citation. In 2 Corinthians 5:8 Origen omits Paul’s ‘μᾶλλον’ (‘rather’) and joins the two verses with his own ‘διό’ (‘therefore’). ‘κακώσεως ... διὰ τὴν κακίαν’ is a wordplay in Greek (affliction / wickedness) that English cannot keep. ‘Adam, that is, man’: Origen glosses the Hebrew name. ‘Ὁ μὲν’ at the start is Celsus; English ‘He’ keeps the Greek.
'sinners are estranged' -> 'sinners were estranged' (aorist ἀπηλλοτριώθησαν, matching 'went astray')
'and in another a vanity "of vanities"' -> 'and in another they are called the vanity "of vanities"' (clearer ellipsis)
Split '(2 Corinthians 5:6, 8)' into one citation beside each quoted clause
